dervis-irab:1-17.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَالطَّارِقِ): originally every one who comes at night, and from it the stars, for their rising at night; and from it Jarīr's saying: "A heart-hunting huntress visited you, and this is not the time for visiting, so go back in peace."
(طرقتك صائدة القلوب وليس ذا ... وقت الزيارة فارجعي بسلام)
Sukayna bint al-Ḥusayn criticised it when she said to Jarīr's reciter: "May Allah make your companion hideous, and make his poetry hideous! What time is more desirable than the nocturnal visit?" It is an active participle from ṭaraqa, ṭarqan and ṭurūqan, when he came by night. What is meant here is the star, and it was called ṭāriq only because of its rising at night. Everyone who came to you by night has ṭaraqaka, and ṭurūq occurs only at night. Hind bint ʿUtba said:
نحن بنات طارق ... نمشي على النمارق
(We are the daughters of Ṭāriq; we walk on the cushions.)
She means that our father is like the star in his loftiness and nobility. The root of al-ṭarq is knocking, and from it the hammer (miṭraqa) was named; the one who seeks the night is called ṭāriq only because he needs to knock (ṭarq) at the door, i.e. strike it, usually; then it was extended to everything that appears at night, whatever it may be; then it was extended to the fullest until it was applied to one who comes by day. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "ṭaraqtu al-bāb ṭarqan (of the pattern qatala); ṭaraqtu al-ḥadīda: I stretched the iron, and ṭarraqtuhā (doubled) for intensity; ṭaraqa al-najm ṭurūqan (of the pattern qaʿada): it rose; everything that came by night has ṭaraqa and is ṭāriq; al-miṭraqa (with kasra) is that with which iron is hammered." As for Ibn Jinnī, he forbade ṭurūq by day. He said: "As for the saying of the common people, 'we seek refuge in Allah from the ṭawāriq of night and day,' it is a mistake, because ṭurūq occurs only at night; the correct form is to say 'we seek refuge in Allah from the ṭawāriq of the night and the jawāriḥ of the day,' because the Arabs say ṭaraqahu when one came to him by night and jaraḥahu when one came by day." In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-ṭāriq: the star called the star of dawn."
(الثَّاقِبُ): the shining, because it pierces the darkness. Abū ʿUbayda said: the Arabs say "athqib nārak," i.e. light your fire. It was also said that al-thāqib is the high; one says thaqaba al-ṭāʾir when it rose in the air, asaffa when it drew near the earth, and dawwama when it stilled its wings to soar. The wording of al-Asās and al-Lisān: thaqaba al-shayʾ bi-l-mithqab; thaqaba al-qidāḥ ʿaynahu to let the descending water out; thaqqaba al-liʾāl al-durr; durr muthaqqab; "he has the pearls of maidens not pierced"; and "they pierced the face veils for their eyes." Al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī said:
أرين محاسنا وكننّ أخرى ... وثقبن الوصاوص للعيون
(They showed some charms and hid others, and pierced the eye-slits for the eyes.)
and by it al-Muthaqqib was named. By figurative use: a bright star (kawkab thāqib) and durrī, very bright and sparkling, as if it pierces the darkness and penetrates it and repels it; and a man thāqib al-raʾy when he is sound and discerning; thaqaba al-ṭāʾir when it soars as if piercing the sky; and thaqqaba al-shayb fī al-liḥya: grey hair began on its forelocks. The pattern of all of them is dakhala.
(الصُّلْبِ): the hard; one says "he is ṣulb in his religion"; "a shepherd ṣulb al-ʿaṣā," when he is harsh with camels; and a bone in the back having vertebrae, stretching from the shoulder to the coccyx or the lower back, plural aṣlāb, aṣlub and ṣulba, and this is what is meant here. One says "he is from the ṣulb of so-and-so," i.e. from his descendants and children. It has four dialectal forms: with damma on the ṣād and sukūn on the lām, al-ṣalab (two fatḥas), and al-ṣulub (two dammas); all were read, and there is a fourth form, al-ṣāliib. «[Translator's note: the source lists the forms as written; the fourth form is printed "الصالب" in the source.]»
(وَالتَّرائِبِ): al-tarāʾib are the bones of the chest where the necklace lies; on the authority of ʿIkrima, al-tarāʾib is what is between the breasts of the woman; and al-Zajjāj related that al-tarāʾib are four ribs on the right of the chest and four ribs on the left of the chest. In the Ḥadīth: "The child is created from the man's water, from his ṣulb come the bone and sinew, and from the woman's water, from her tarāʾib come the flesh and blood." In al-Mukhtār: "al-tarāʾib is the plural of tarība like ṣaḥīfa and ṣaḥāʾif." Imruʾ al-Qays said:
مهفهفة بيضاء غير مفاضة ... ترائبها مصقولة كالسجنجل
(Slender, white, not flabby; her breastbones polished like a mirror.)
meaning the mirror. One also says tarīb without the hāʾ. It was recited for al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī:
ومن ذهب يلوح على تريب ... كلون العاج ليس بذي غضون
(And of gold gleaming on a breastbone like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles.)
More of its meaning will come in the section on Rhetoric.
(السَّرائِرُ): what is kept secret in the hearts of beliefs and intentions, and what is hidden of deeds; its testing (balāʾ) is knowing them, examining them, and distinguishing the good from the foul among them. On the authority of al-Ḥasan, he heard a man reciting:
سيبقى لها في مضمر القلب والحشا ... سريرة ودّ يوم تبلى السرائر
(There will remain for her in the hidden heart and the innards a secret love, on the day when secrets are tested.)
and he said: "How heedless he is of what is in sūrat al-samāʾ wa-l-ṭāriq!" In al-Mukhtār: "al-sirr is what is concealed, plural asrār; al-sarīra is like it, plural sarāʾir."
(الرَّجْعِ): the rain, because it returns every so often; the clouds carry the water from the rains and then return it to the earth. It is also called awb because it returns (yaʾūbu). Al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhalī said:
رباء شماء لا يأوي لقلتها ... إلا السحاب وإلا الأوب والسبل
(A lookout of a lofty fortress, to whose summit nothing resorts but the clouds, and the rain, and the downpour.)
He laments his son or describes a man as a rabbāʾ, i.e. a climber, from rabaʾa and irtabaʾa when he climbed to look at something, and from it al-rabīʾa (the sentinel); its annexation to shammāʾ is the annexation of the description to its object, and it is the high fortress, from al-shamam, which is height; and al-qulla is the highest of a mountain and its peak. Al-awb is the rain, so called because its origin is from the waters of the seas, and then it returns to them; and al-sabal (vowelled) is the rain, from asbaltu al-sitr when I let it down and loosened it. Al-Wāḥidī said: "al-rajʿ is the rain, in the view of all the exegetes."
(الصَّدْعِ): the split, because it cracks the earth and it is cracked by it. In al-Asās: "and the earth cracked with plants, and Allah the Exalted split it: ﴿وَالْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ الصَّدْعِ﴾."

* I'rab:
(وَالسَّماءِ وَالطَّارِقِ وَما أَدْراكَ مَا الطَّارِقُ النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ إِنْ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَمَّا عَلَيْها حافِظٌ)
The wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; السَّماءِ is genitive by the wāw of oath; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted verb of oath; الطَّارِقِ is also an oath, joined to what precedes; the wāw is a conjunction; ما is an interrogative noun, mubtadaʾ, and the clause أَدْراكَ is its khabar; ما is an interrogative noun and الطَّارِقُ is its khabar; the clause suspended by the interrogative fills the place of the second object of أَدْراكَ; النَّجْمُ is a badal of الطَّارِقُ, or the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, as if it were an answer to the question preceding it, for magnification. The clause إِنْ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَمَّا عَلَيْها حافِظٌ has no grammatical position because it is the response to the oath, and what lies between the oath and its response is parenthetical. إِنْ lightened is negative; كُلُّ نَفْسٍ is a mubtadaʾ; لَمَّا with shadda means "illā"; عَلَيْها is a fronted khabar and حافِظٌ a deferred mubtadaʾ; the nominal clause is the khabar of كُلُّ. It was also read لَمَا lightened, in which case the lām is the distinguishing lām (al-lām al-fāriqa) and إِنْ is lightened from the heavy and inoperative, and ما is redundant. Ibn Mālik pointed to this in al-Khulāṣa, saying:
وخففت إن فقل العمل ... وتلزم اللام إذا ما تهمل
(Inna is lightened, and its operation becomes rare, and the lām is obligatory when it is left inoperative.)
A parallel has already been given in Yā Sīn. (فَلْيَنْظُرِ الْإِنْسانُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ؟ خُلِقَ مِنْ ماءٍ دافِقٍ، يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بَيْنِ الصُّلْبِ وَالتَّرائِبِ): the fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; the lām is the lām of command; يَنْظُرِ is an imperfect verb jussive by the lām; الْإِنْسانُ is the agent. مِمَّ: مِنْ is a preposition and ما an interrogative noun in the position of a genitive after مِنْ; it has already been noted that the interrogative ما may drop its alif if a preposition precedes it. The preposition and its genitive noun are attached to خُلِقَ; the clause خُلِقَ is in the position of an accusative for فَلْيَنْظُرِ, which is suspended from it by the interrogative; the answer to the interrogative is خُلِقَ مِنْ ماءٍ. The clause خُلِقَ مِنْ ماءٍ دافِقٍ is resumptive, as if an answer to an implied question; خُلِقَ is a passive past verb; مِنْ ماءٍ is attached to خُلِقَ; دافِقٍ is a naʿt of ماءٍ, i.e. "poured out" (madfūq), or it is of the forms of relation (nisba), like lābin and tāmir, or it is figurative by attribution, attributing to the water what belongs to its owner, for emphasis. The clause يَخْرُجُ is a second naʿt, or a ḥāl; مِنْ بَيْنِ الصُّلْبِ is attached to يَخْرُجُ; التَّرائِبِ is conjoined to الصُّلْبِ. (إِنَّهُ عَلى رَجْعِهِ لَقادِرٌ يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرائِرُ فَما لَهُ مِنْ قُوَّةٍ وَلا ناصِرٍ): إن and its noun; عَلى رَجْعِهِ is attached to قادِرٌ; the pronoun in إنه refers to Allah; the shifted lām; قادِرٌ is the khabar of إن; يَوْمَ is an adverbial attached to رَجْعِهِ; it is not sound to attach it to قادِرٌ because He the Exalted is able to bring him back at every time and His power is not specific to one time rather than another. It was also said that it is governed by an omitted verb, its implied form being "yarjiʿuhu yawma" or "udhkur yawma" (mention the day), and perhaps that is preferable. Some said it is attached to ناصِرٍ, which is unsound, because what follows the negative ما and what follows the fāʾ does not act on what precedes them. The fāʾ is a conjunction; ما is negative; لَهُ is a fronted khabar; مِنْ is a redundant preposition and قُوَّةٍ is genitive in form by مِنْ and nominative in position, being the deferred mubtadaʾ; the wāw is a conjunction; لا is negative and ناصِرٍ is conjoined to قُوَّةٍ; the clause تُبْلَى السَّرائِرُ is in the position of a genitive by the annexation of the adverbial to it; السَّرائِرُ is the deputy agent of تُبْلَى. (وَالسَّماءِ ذاتِ الرَّجْعِ وَالْأَرْضِ ذاتِ الصَّدْعِ): the wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; السَّماءِ is genitive by the wāw of oath; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the omitted verb of oath; ذاتِ الرَّجْعِ is a naʿt of السَّماءِ; الْأَرْضِ ذاتِ الصَّدْعِ is conjoined to the preceding clause. (إِنَّهُ لَقَوْلٌ فَصْلٌ وَما هُوَ بِالْهَزْلِ): the clause has no position because it is the response to the oath; إن and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām, for emphasis; قَوْلٌ is the khabar of إن; فَصْلٌ is a naʿt of قَوْلٌ; the wāw is a conjunction; ما is Ḥijāzī, acting as ليس, and هُوَ is its noun; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition and الْهَزْلِ is genitive in form and accusative in position because it is the khabar of ما. (إِنَّهُمْ يَكِيدُونَ كَيْداً وَأَكِيدُ كَيْداً فَمَهِّلِ الْكافِرِينَ أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْداً): a resumptive utterance, introduced to answer a question arising from the drift of the speech, as if it were said, "And what is the name of their arrogance and obstinacy?" and it was said, "They..." إن and its noun, and the clause يَكِيدُونَ is its khabar; كَيْداً is an absolute object; the fāʾ is eloquent, i.e. "if you wish to see the outcome of their affair, do not hasten to take vengeance on them"; مَهِّلِ is an imperative verb; الْكافِرِينَ is a direct object; أَمْهِلْهُمْ: he repeated the imperative as emphasis to His Messenger, and increased the form to further calm his heart and make him patient; رُوَيْداً is accusative as a maṣdar, the original being irwād, so it is a diminutive of abbreviation (taṣghīr tarkhīm) by dropping the extra letters. In al-Mukhtār: "'so-and-so is on rawd' (like ʿawd), i.e. on leisure, and its diminutive is ruwayd; one says arwada fī al-sayr, irwādan and murwadan (with damma or fatḥa on the mīm), meaning gently; and you say "ruwaydaka ʿAmran," i.e. give him time; it is a diminutive of abbreviation from irwād, the maṣdar of arwada yurwidu." The wording of al-Samīn: "Know that ruwaydan is used as a maṣdar in place of the wording of its verb, so it is sometimes annexed, as in ﴿فَضَرْبَ الرِّقابِ﴾, and sometimes not annexed, as in 'ruwaydan Zaydan'; it occurs as a ḥāl, as in 'they travelled ruwaydan,' i.e. slowly; and as an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, as in 'they travelled ruwaydan,' i.e. a gentle travelling." Further, ruwayd in "ruwayd Zaydan" comes as a verbal noun (ism fiʿl) meaning "give him time," derived from its named verb, which is arwada, whose origin is the maṣdar irwād, diminished by dropping the extra letters as a diminutive of abbreviation; similarly "tayd Zaydan" in the sense of "ruwayd Zaydan." What we see is that if it is annexed, it is a verbal noun of the imperative, indeclinable on fatḥa, with no grammatical position, and its agent is a latent pronoun whose implied form is "you"; if you put tanwīn on it, as in "ruwaydan akhāka," or annex them, as in "ruwayda akhīka," it is then accusative as an absolute object. «[Translator's note: the source says "if it is annexed it is a verbal noun" and then "if you put tanwīn on it or annex them"; the wording is rendered as written.]»

* Rhetoric:
1- In «من بين الصلب والترائب» there is a ṭibāq (antithesis): he set the bone of the back against the bone of the chest, and made the first singular and the other plural because the chest of the woman is her tarība, so one says of the woman "tarāʾib," meaning the tarība and what is around it and what surrounds it; likewise the Arabs say, "I saw the woman's anklets and her breast," though she has only two breasts and two anklets. Or it is said that He the Exalted meant "it comes out from between the backbones and the breastbones," and made do with the singular in place of the plural, as the Exalted said: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أَنَّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضَ كانَتا رَتْقاً فَفَتَقْناهُما﴾, and He did not say "and the earths." Abū al-Ṭayyib gazed at the sky of this verse and transferred it in a subtle transfer that attests to ability and brilliance, saying in love poetry, and did well:
بأبي الشموس الجانحات غواربا ... اللابسات من الحرير جلاببا
المنهبات قلوبنا وعقولنا ... وجناتهنّ الناهبات الناهبا
الناعمات القاتلات المحييا ... ت المبديات من الدلال غرائبا
حاولن تفديتي وخفن مراقبا ... فوضعن أيديهنّ فوق ترائبا
وبسمن عن برد خشيت أذيبه ... من حر أنفاسي فكنت الذائبا
(By my father, the suns inclining at their setting, wearing garments of silk, plundering our hearts and minds, their cheeks plundering the plunderer; the soft ones, the killers, the life-givers, who show strange coquetries. They tried to say "may we ransom you," but feared a watcher, so they put their hands upon their breastbones; and they smiled, showing hail which I feared I would melt with the heat of my breaths, and I was the one who melted.)
We cited the passage only for its fineness. The point is in the fourth verse, where he borrowed the location of the woman's desire and made them put their hands on it; for this reason none of the commentators on Abū al-Ṭayyib's dīwān could understand the verse in its reality, and they muddled it wondrously. Ibn Jinnī said: "They signalled to me from afar and did not say the greeting aloud for fear of watchers and slanderers," and this is not intelligible speech, for fear of slanderers and watchers calls for putting the hands on the faces, not on the breastbones. Al-Wāḥidī, who wandered in a desert of delusion, said: "They wanted to say 'we ransom you with ourselves' and feared the watcher, so they moved the ransoming from speech to gesture, i.e. 'ourselves ransom you,'" and this makes the speech bear what it cannot bear. Perhaps Ibn Fūrja was cleverer than his two companions, for he said: "Putting the hand on the chest is not a gesture of greeting; he meant that they put their hands over their breastbones to calm the hearts from palpitation"; though, for all its fineness, it is contradicted by the first half of the verse. «[Translator's note: the source calls the verse the "fourth" and the line citing "فوق ترائبا" is as printed there.]»
2- In «النجم الثاقب» there is separation (faṣl), whereas the flow of the speech calls for conjunction, because he intended to share them in the ruling and they agreed on it; he turned from it only to magnify its importance. He first swore by what is shared by it and others, namely al-ṭāriq; then asked about it with the interrogative to magnify its importance a second time; then explained it as the star, to remove that vagueness produced by the interrogative. It is reported that Abū Ṭālib was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when a star fell, and Abū Ṭālib was alarmed and said, "What is this?" He, peace be upon him, said: "This is a star that has been hurled, and it is one of the signs of Allah."
3- In «والسماء والطارق وما أدراك ما الطارق النجم الثاقب إن كل نفس لما عليها حافظ» there is the art of mumāthala, which is the parallelism of the words of the speech, all or some of them, in weight without rhyme; so al-ṭāriq, al-thāqib and ḥāfiẓ are parallel in weight without rhyme. Some of the words of mumāthala sometimes come rhymed without intention, as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
كأن المدام وصوب الغمام ... وريح الخزامى ونشر العطر
(As if the wine and the downpour of the clouds, and the scent of lavender and the diffusion of perfume...)
Shaykh ʿAbd al-Ghanī al-Nābulusī cited two verses by the judge Yaḥyā ibn Aktham on mumāthala:
إنما الدنيا طعام ... ومدام وغلام
فإذا فاتك هذا ... فعلى الدنيا السلام
(The world is only food, wine and a youth; if you miss these, then farewell to the world.)
and he cited for Ibn al-Ṣāʾigh also:
زار الحبيب بليلة ... ووشاته لم يشعروا
فضممته ولثمته ... وفعلت ما لا يذكر
(The beloved visited by night while his slanderers were unaware; I embraced him and kissed him, and did what is not mentioned.)
For this reason Ibn Ḥijja said of the art of mumāthala that it is a low type in relation to the others.

* Benefits:
Responses to the oath (ajwibat al-qasam):
The responses to the oath are four: inna, mā, the lām and lā. Two particles affirm, and they are inna and the lām; two negate, and they are mā and lā, as in your saying "By Allah, Zayd did not stand" and "By Allah, Zayd did stand."
